attempts.raw_response: Wait two to three days for the cut ends to dry and callus over. This step is essential because wet cuttings are far more likely to rot once placed in soil. Once the ends have formed a firm callus, fill a small pot with a well draining cactus or succulent mix. Dip the callused end into rooting hormone if desired, then insert it about an inch deep into the soil. Water sparingly at first, just enough to moisten the surrounding soil without soaking it. Place the pot in a warm spot with bright, indirect light. Within four to six weeks, gentle resistance when you tug the stem indicates roots have begun forming.

pair.human_continuation: They should be dried out and ready to use within 2 days. Peat moss and sand create a well-draining planting medium. You can substitute the sand with fine gravel or perlite for a similar effect. Lay a thin layer of gravel on the bottom of the pot so the pot drains more efficiently. You can use a store-bought mixture meant for cacti or succulents if you do not want to mix your own. The cuttings can be kept indoors or outdoors as long as they stay in a warm and bright place, but keep them out of direct sunlight. As they begin to sprout new leaves, you can begin moving the adeniums into more direct sunlight.
pair.prefix: Pick a healthy stem at least 6 inches (15 cm) long. Use a sharp pair of pruning shears to cut the stem where it where it connects to the trunk. One pruning session can result in many stems that you can propagate into their own adenium plants! Lay the cut stems on a newspaper or paper towel and keep them out of direct sunlight. Store them in a place that is warm but is not humid.
